'''John Allan Chapman''' (July 14, 1965 – March 4, 2002) was a [[United States Air Force Combat Control Team|combat controller]] in the [[United States Air Force]] who was [[posthumous award|posthumously]] awarded the [[Medal of Honor]] on August 22, 2018, for his actions in the [[Battle of Takur Ghar]] during the [[War in Afghanistan (2001–present)|War in Afghanistan]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.dodlive.mil/2018/08/20/fallen-airman-earning-moh-was-top-performer-tenacious-fighter/|title=Fallen airman earning MoH|date=August 20, 2018|website=defense.mil|access-date=August 20, 2018}}</ref> He is the first airman to receive the Medal of Honor since the [[Vietnam War]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.military.com/daily-news/2018/04/20/report-fallen-air-force-tech-sgt-approved-medal-honor.html|title=Report: Fallen Air Force Tech Sgt. Approved for Medal of Honor|date=April 20, 2018|website=Military.com|access-date=May 29, 2018}}</ref> He was inducted into the [[The Pentagon#Hall of Heroes|Hall of Heroes]] on August 23, 2018, and posthumously promoted to [[Master Sergeant]] on the following day.

Chapman was also the first Air Force [[United States Air Force Combat Control Team|combat controller]] to be awarded the [[Air Force Cross (United States)|Air Force Cross]] before his decoration was upgraded to the Medal of Honor.<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://www.ccshf.org/portfolio-view/tsgt-john-chapman/|title=TSgt John Chapman – CCSHF|work=CCSHF|access-date=April 21, 2018|language=en-US}}</ref>

==Early life==
John Chapman was born July 14, 1965, in [[Springfield, Massachusetts]], to Eugene and Terry Chapman and grew up in [[Windsor Locks, Connecticut]].<ref name="auto">{{Cite web|url=http://veterantributes.org/TributeDetail.php?recordID=442|title=Veteran Tributes|website=Veterantributes.org|access-date=April 21, 2018}}</ref> He has two sisters, Lori and Tammy, and a brother, Kevin. He graduated from Windsor Locks High School in 1983.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://patch.com/connecticut/windsorlocks/fallen-windsor-locks-solider-awarded-medal-honor|title=Fallen Windsor Locks Soldier Awarded Medal Of Honor|date=2018-08-22|work=Windsor Locks-East Windsor, CT Patch|access-date=2018-08-23|language=en-US}}</ref>

==Military career==
===Information Systems Operator===
[[File:Airman to be awarded Medal of Honor 180727-F-F3227-1001.jpg|thumb|190px|left|Chapman in Afghanistan]]
Chapman enlisted in the [[United States Air Force]] on September 27, 1985, and was trained as an information systems operator. His first assignment was with the 1987th Information Systems Squadron at [[Lowry Air Force Base]], [[Colorado]], from February 1986 to June 1989.

===Combat Control Operator===
Chapman cross-trained into the [[United States Air Force Combat Control Team|Combat Control]] career field and served with the [[21st Special Tactics Squadron|1721st Combat Control Squadron]] at [[Pope Field|Pope Air Force Base]], [[North Carolina]], from August 1990 to November 1992.{{r|auto}}

He was a Special Tactics team member with the [[320th Special Tactics Squadron]] at [[Kadena Air Base]] on [[Okinawa Island|Okinawa]] from November 1992 to October 1995. His final assignment was with the [[24th Special Tactics Squadron]] at Pope Air Force Base.{{r|auto}}

===Operation Enduring Freedom===
[[File:Technical Sergeant John Chapman.jpg|thumb|Chapman geared for a parachute jump]]
[[File:Johnchapmanafghansafehouse.jpg|thumb|right|Chapman with an Afghan girl in a safehouse in Afghanistan]]
On March 4, 2002, Chapman and members of the [[SEAL Team Six|United States Navy SEAL Team Six]] took part in [[Operation Anaconda]]. A [[Boeing MH-47 Chinook]]<ref>{{Cite book|title=To the Top of Takur Gar|last=Kitfield|first=James|publisher=AIR FORCE Magazine|year=2011|url=http://www.airforcemag.com/MagazineArchive/Documents/2011/July%202011/0711takurgar.pdf|pages=52}}</ref> came under enemy fire, causing Navy SEAL Neil C. Roberts to fall. The helicopter landed {{convert|4.5|mi}} away from where Roberts was killed.<ref name=Handbook>{{Cite web|url=http://static.e-publishing.af.mil/production/1/af_a1/publication/afhandbook1/afhandbook1.pdf|title=The Airman Handbook|date=October 1, 2017|website=Static.e-publishing.af.mil|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180421162941/http://static.e-publishing.af.mil/production/1/af_a1/publication/afhandbook1/afhandbook1.pdf|archive-date=April 21, 2018|access-date=April 20, 2018}}</ref> Once on the ground, Chapman called for air support protection until another helicopter could pick them up. He and the team volunteered to rescue Roberts from the enemy stronghold.

Upon returning to recover Roberts, the team came under fire from three directions. Chapman charged forward, killing two enemy soldiers and advancing towards a defensive fighting in Bunker 1<ref name=Handbook /> from minimal personal cover, and he received multiple wounds. His engagement and destruction of the first enemy position and advancement to the second enabled his team to move to cover and break enemy contact. He is credited with saving the lives of the entire SEAL Team Six team.<ref name=Handbook />

Once Bunker 1 was clear, Chapman was hit and went down. His SEAL team leader, Britt Slabinski, failing to check Chapman for signs of life, ordered his SEAL teammates to retreat down the mountain, leaving Chapman alone. Despite being mortally wounded, Chapman came to and engaged enemy combatants at Bunker 2 for an hour and twenty minutes. He sustained gunshot wounds, shrapnel wounds, cuts and bruises from hand-to-hand combat, and concussive injuries from the American bombs called to his position by Slabinski. With the morning in full light, Chapman heard another incoming Chinook. It was the Quick Reaction Force (QRF) called in by Slabinski. Chapman knew it would suffer the same fate as the first two helos, which would likely result in many American deaths, if not all aboard. Knowing that the enemy wanted his position, he made the decision to leave cover in order to protect the QRF with suppressive fire. As he lay prone, firing at an entrenched machine gun position, an enemy fighter fired the round that ultimately killed him. Though five men from the QRF were killed, Chapman's actions allowed those on the helo time to defend their location and saved lives.<ref>{{Cite AV media |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3oKMjTqdTYo&si=Yth1De82VEV9VQXm |title=The First Medal of Honor Ever Recorded |date=2019-06-26 |last=Dan Schilling Books |access-date=2025-01-17 |via=YouTube}}</ref>{{Unreliable source?|date=July 2025|reason=WP:NOYT}}<ref>{{Cite book |last=Schilling |first=Dan |title=Alone at dawn: Medal of Honor Recipient John Chapman and the untold story of the world's deadliest special operations force |last2=Longfritz |first2=Lori Chapman |date=2019 |publisher=Grand Central Publishing |isbn=978-1-5387-2965-6 |edition=First |location=New York}}</ref>

==Air Force Cross upgraded to the Medal of Honor==
Chapman was posthumously awarded the Air Force Cross. The citation for the award reads:
{{blockquote|The President of the United States of America, authorized by Title 10, Section 8742, U.S.C., awards the Air Force Cross to TSgt John Chapman for extraordinary heroism in military operation against an armed enemy of the United States as a 24th Special Tactics Squadron, combat controller in the vicinity of Gardez, in the eastern highlands of Afghanistan, on March 4, 2002. On this date, during his helicopter insertion for a reconnaissance and time sensitive targeting close air support mission, Sergeant Chapman's aircraft came under heavy machine gun fire and received a direct hit from a rocket propelled grenade which caused a United States Navy sea-air-land team member to fall from the aircraft. Though heavily damaged, the aircraft egressed the area and made an emergency landing seven kilometers away. Once on the ground Sergeant Chapman established communication with an AC-130 gunship to ensure the area was secure while providing close air support coverage for the entire team. He then directed the gunship to begin the search for the missing team member. He requested, coordinated, and controlled the helicopter that extracted the stranded team and aircrew members. These actions limited the exposure of the aircrew and team to hostile fire. Without regard for his own life Sergeant Chapman volunteered to rescue his missing team member from an enemy stronghold. Shortly after insertion, the team made contact with the enemy. Sergeant Chapman engaged and killed two enemy personnel. He continued to advance reaching the enemy position then engaged a second enemy position, a dug-in machine gun nest. At this time, the rescue team came under effective enemy fire from three directions. From close range he exchanged fire with the enemy from minimum personal cover until he succumbed to multiple wounds. His engagement and destruction of the first enemy position and advancement on the second position enabled his team to move to cover and break enemy contact. In his own words, his Navy sea-air-land team leader credits Sergeant Chapman unequivocally with saving the lives of the entire rescue team. Through his extraordinary heroism, superb airmanship, aggressiveness in the face of the enemy, and the dedication to the service of his country, Sergeant Chapman reflects the highest credit upon himself and the United States Air Force.}}

[[File:Air_Force_Cross_Medal.svg|thumb|right|100px|Air Force Cross]]
Fourteen years after Chapman's death,<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.military.com/daily-news/2016/08/28/air-force-seeks-medal-honor-ct-native-who-died-afghanistan.html|title=Air Force Seeks Medal of Honor for Sergeant Who Died in 2002|work=Military.com|access-date=April 21, 2018|language=en}}</ref> Air Force Secretary [[Deborah Lee James]] began attempting to have Chapman awarded the Medal of Honor, the military's highest award, after new technology that allowed a deeper analysis of video of the battle suggested Chapman regained consciousness and resumed fighting [[Al-Qaeda]] members who were coming toward him from three directions. Chapman may have crawled into a bunker, shot and killed an enemy charging at him and then killed another enemy fighter in hand-to-hand combat.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.airforcetimes.com/news/your-air-force/2016/08/29/congressman-tsgt-chapman-deserves-the-medal-of-honor/|title=Congressman: TSgt Chapman deserves the Medal of Honor|last=Losey|first=Stephen|date=August 7, 2017|work=Air Force Times|access-date=April 21, 2018|language=en-US}}</ref>

While the Air Force pushed for Chapman to be recognized, [[United States Naval Special Warfare Command|Naval Special Warfare Command]] allegedly attempted to block Chapman's Medal of Honor as it would result in an admission that Chapman had been left behind.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://greydynamics.com/the-24th-special-tactics-squadron/ | title=24th Special Tactics Squadron: Spear of the Sky }}</ref> When it became apparent that Chapman's Medal of Honor could not be blocked, it was further alleged that the Navy put the commander of the operation, [[Britt K. Slabinski]], up for the same award, which he received in May 2018.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.newsweek.com/2018/05/18/navy-seals-seal-team-6-left-behind-die-operation-anaconda-slabinski-chapman-912343.html|title=The Navy SEALs Allegedly Left Behind a Man in Afghanistan. Did They Also Try to Block His Medal of Honor?|last=Naylor|first=Sean D.|date=May 7, 2018|work=Newsweek|access-date=July 27, 2018}}</ref> In March 2018, Chapman's family was notified that his Air Force Cross was to be upgraded to the Medal of Honor.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://taskandpurpose.com/john-chapman-medal-honor-afghanistan/|title=John Chapman To Be First Airman Since Vietnam To Receive Medal Of Honor|last=Szoldra|first=Paul|date=April 20, 2018|work=Task & Purpose|access-date=April 21, 2018|language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.military.com/daily-news/2018/08/22/moh-recipient-john-chapman-wasnt-left-behind-his-team-family-says.html |title=MoH Recipient John Chapman Wasn't Left Behind by His Team, Family Says |last=Pawlyk |first=Oriana |date=22 Aug 2018|website=Military.com|access-date=5 Jul 2020|language=en-US}}</ref>

The citation accompanying his upgrade to the Medal of Honor reads as follows:<ref name=Museum>{{cite web |title=Tech. Sgt. John A. Chapman |url=https://www.nationalmuseum.af.mil/Visit/Museum-Exhibits/Fact-Sheets/Display/Article/196830/tech-sgt-john-a-chapman/ |publisher=National Museum of the US Air Force |access-date=27 August 2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://taskandpurpose.com/john-chapman-medal-of-honor-citation/|title=Read The Full Citation For Air Force Tech Sgt. John Chapman's Medal Of Honor|date=August 22, 2018|website=Task & Purpose|access-date=August 25, 2018}}</ref>

{{blockquote|Technical Sergeant John A. Chapman distinguished himself by extraordinary heroism as an Air Force Special Tactics combat controller, attached to a Navy Sea, Air, and Land (SEAL) Team conducting reconnaissance operations in Takur Ghar, Afghanistan, on March 4, 2002. During insertion, the team's helicopter was ambushed causing a teammate to fall into an entrenched group of enemy combatants below. Sergeant Chapman and the team voluntarily reinserted onto the snow-capped mountain, into the heart of a known enemy stronghold to rescue one of their own. Without regard for his own safety, Sergeant Chapman immediately engaged, moving in the direction of the closest enemy position despite coming under heavy fire from multiple directions. He fearlessly charged an enemy bunker, up a steep incline in thigh-deep snow and into hostile fire, directly engaging the enemy. Upon reaching the bunker, Sergeant Chapman assaulted and cleared the position, killing all enemy occupants. With complete disregard for his own life, Sergeant Chapman deliberately moved from cover only 12 meters from the enemy, and exposed himself once again to attack a second bunker, from which an emplaced machine gun was firing on his team. During this assault from an exposed position directly in the line of intense fire, Sergeant Chapman was struck and injured by enemy fire. Despite severe, mortal wounds, he continued to fight relentlessly, sustaining a violent engagement with multiple enemy personnel before making the ultimate sacrifice. By his heroic actions and extraordinary valor, sacrificing his life for the lives of his teammates, Technical Sergeant Chapman upheld the highest traditions of military service and reflected great credit upon himself and the United States Air Force.}}

[[File:Air Force - Medal of Honor (16285785564).jpg|alt=Air Force Medal of Honor|thumb|100px|right|Medal of Honor]]
The ceremony took place Wednesday, August 22, 2018.<ref>‘How incredible the sacrifice:' In the chaos of an Afghanistan battle, John Chapman's heroism was clear; August 22, 2018; https://www.airforcetimes.com/news/your-air-force/2018/08/22/how-incredible-the-sacrifice-in-the-chaos-of-an-afghanistan-battle-john-chapmans-heroism-was-clear/</ref> At an August 23 ceremony at the Pentagon attended by family and teammates, Chapman was inducted into the Hall of Heroes, a room dedicated to honor Medal of Honor recipients.<ref>What is the Hall of Heroes?; MARCH 20, 2019; https://www.war.gov/News/Feature-Stories/Story/Article/1774933/what-is-the-hall-of-heroes/</ref> The next day, he was posthumously promoted to the rank of Master Sergeant and his name was added to the Medal of Honor wall at the [[United States Air Force Memorial|Air Force Memorial]].

==Personal life==
Chapman met Valerie Novak in 1990 while he and a friend were visiting her hometown of [[Windber, Pennsylvania]]. They married in 1992 and had two daughters, Madison and Brianna.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.yahoo.com/news/airman-john-chapman-apos-widow-193249746.html|title=Airman John Chapman's Widow Speaks Out as He's Awarded Posthumous Medal of Honor: 'It's Very Humbling'|date=August 22, 2018}}</ref>
Chapman is buried at Saint Mary's Byzantine Catholic Church Cemetery in Windber.

==Legacy==
Chapman's actions in the Battle of Takur Ghar were recorded from multiple angles from circling aircraft and are reported to be the first Medal of Honor actions ever recorded on video.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://taskandpurpose.com/military-life/john-chapman-video-medal-honor/|title=Watch John Chapman's incredible heroics in the first Medal of Honor action ever recorded on video|last=Szoldra|first=Paul|date=March 4, 2021|work=Task & Purpose|access-date=February 28, 2024}}</ref>

The [[Military Sealift Command]] logistics ship {{MV|TSgt John A. Chapman|T-AK-323}} was renamed in his honor in 2005.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.msc.navy.mil/sealift/2005/april/chapman.htm|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061214191054/http://www.msc.navy.mil/sealift/2005/April/chapman.htm|url-status=dead|archive-date=December 14, 2006|title=Ship named for USAF hero|date=April 2005|website=U.S. Navy's Military Sealift Command|access-date=July 28, 2018}}</ref>

Dan Schilling and Chapman's sister, Lori Chapman Longfritz, wrote a book based on his Medal of Honor action titled ''Alone at Dawn: Medal of Honor Recipient John Chapman and the Untold Story of the World's Deadliest Special Operations Force''.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Schilling |first1=Dan |title=Alone at dawn: Medal of Honor recipient John Chapman and the untold story of the world's deadliest special operations force |last2=Longfritz |first2=Lori Chapman |date=June 25, 2019 |publisher=Grand Central Publishing |isbn=978-1-5387-2965-6 |edition=1st}}</ref> It has also been optioned for a feature adaptation by Thruline Entertainment.<ref>{{cite web |last=Busch |first=Anita |date=May 23, 2018 |title=Military Hero John Chapman's Incredible Story To Come To Big Screen, Courtesy Of Thruline Entertainment |url=https://deadline.com/2018/05/air-force-hero-john-chapmans-movie-book-afghanistan-thruline-entertainment-1202396617/ |publisher=}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Untitled John Chapman Project |url=https://www.imdb.com/title/tt8483914/reference |publisher= |via=www.imdb.com}}</ref> In 2021, it was revealed the film would be called ''Combat Control'', directed by [[Ron Howard]].<ref>{{Citation |last=Hargrave |first=Sam |title=Combat Control |url=https://www.imdb.com/title/tt8483914/ |type=Thriller, War |publisher=The Hideaway Entertainment, Thruline Entertainment |access-date=2022-09-05}}</ref> In October 2025, it was announced that the film was retitled to ''[[Alone at Dawn]]'',  will star [[Adam Driver]] as John Chapman and [[Anne Hathaway]] as Lori Chapman Longfirtz, with Ron Howard directing.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Kroll |first=Justin |date=2025-10-03 |title=Adam Driver & Anne Hathaway To Star In Military Drama ‘Alone At Dawn’ From Ron Howard And Amazon MGM Studios |url=https://deadline.com/2025/10/adam-driver-anne-hathaway-alone-at-dawn-ron-howard-1236568655/ |access-date=2026-05-20 |website=Deadline |language=en-US}}</ref> Filming commenced in November 2025 and wrapped in February 2026.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Dutta |first=Shubhabrata |date=2025-10-15 |title=Ron Howard's 'Alone at Dawn' Starts Filming in Maryland and Budapest in November |url=https://thecinemaholic.com/alone-at-dawn-filming/ |access-date=2026-05-20 |website=The Cinemaholic |language=en-US}}</ref> 

On April 22, 2023, the [[United States Air Force Academy]] graduating class of 2026 selected MSgt John A. Chapman as their class exemplar, honored with the nickname "Sarge." Chapman is the first enlisted to be chosen by an Academy graduating class.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uwZD0JyIyeE&ab_channel=USAFAClassof2026|title=USAFA Class of 2026 Exemplar Reveal|date=April 22, 2023|website=YouTube|access-date=May 16, 2023}}</ref>

According to retired green beret Nate Cornacchia in a post on [[YouTube]], the upcoming Medal of Honor museum in Arlington, Texas was going to have an exhibit dedicated to John Chapman but has since been canceled and replaced with [[Britt K. Slabinski|Britt Slabinski]], who is on the museum board. Per Chapman's sister, Lori Chapman Longfritz, the museum gave her a tour in February 2024 while it was being built. She was shown where John's exhibit would be and she offered artifacts from the family. In November 2024, she learned that the museum would not in fact be honoring Chapman ... the first airman to receive the Medal of Honor since Vietnam and the first to be recorded. Instead, they chose to reduce Chapman to a photo on the wall and an edited and muted version of the historic drone video. Slabinski, whose citation credits him with Chapman's actions, is showcased with an enormous exhibit including a glass case with two uniforms: his white Navy uniform and the one he allegedly wore during the battle. There are supposedly bullet holes in the leg, however Slabinski never suffered any injuries. The museum honors every recipient on the anniversaries of their birthdays. On July 14, 2025, the museum failed to remember Chapman's birthday. The Navy SEALs appear to be attempting to distance Slabinski from Chapman, even though he would probably not be alive were it not for Chapman.<ref>{{Cite AV media |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=atn4PcWygLU&si=cJQStvCJsBBFzCdI |title=Navy SEALs Dishonor John Chapman AGAIN. This is DISGUSTING. 🚨NEW🚨 |date=2025-01-12 |last=Valhalla VFT |access-date=2025-01-17 |via=YouTube}}</ref>{{Better source needed|date=February 2025}}<ref>{{Cite web |title=Critics say Medal of Honor museum shortchanges airman’s achievements |url=https://www.stripes.com/veterans/2025-02-10/medal-of-honor-museum-petition-16783333.html |access-date=2025-02-11 |website=Stars and Stripes |language=en}}</ref>
